parole.testo: From calque of German beruhen (older form also berugen) or Middle Low German *berouwen, equivalent to be- + ro. Cognate with Danish bero and Norwegian Bokmål bero.

parole.significato: to give the right (to), to entitle
parole.testo: From German berechtigen, from Middle Low German berichten. Cognate with Danish berettige, Norwegian Bokmål berettige. Equivalent to be- + rätt + -iga.

parole.significato: to give, to donate, to assign, to divide (unto each his part)
parole.testo: From German bescheren or Middle Low German bescheren, from Old High German biskeran and Old Saxon biskeran respectively, equivalent to be- + skära. Cognate with Danish beskære, Norwegian Bokmål beskjære, Dutch bescheren, West Frisian beskeare, English beshear, Old Frisian biskera and Yiddish באַשערן

parole.significato: to punish, to penalize (inflict a punishment upon, generally or judicially)
parole.testo: From German bestrafen or a corresponding Middle Low German verb. Cognate with Danish bestrafe †, Dutch bestraffen and Middle Low German bestraflik. Equivalent to be- + straffa.
From German Fuchsschwanz or its Middle Low German equivalent.
Likely borrowed from German knipsen, from Middle Low German knippen, from Proto-Germanic *knippōną. Probably related, more distantly, to knipa and nypa.
Sense 1 from German Niet. Sense 2 from Middle Low German nit, from Old Saxon nith. Doublet of nid. Sense 3 from Dutch niet.
Borrowed from German nieten or Middle Low German nêden, from Proto-Germanic *hneudaną. According to SO attested since 1790. In punch and defeat sense; according to SO attested since 1958.

parole.significato: provost: an honorific title for a priest, awarded by the bishop
parole.testo: Via German Propst and/or Middle Low German prōvest from Latin prōpositus.
Borrowed from German Schacht, from Middle Low German schacht, from Old Saxon skaft, from Proto-Germanic *skaftaz. Doublet of skaft and skäkta.
From German Stieglitz and/or Middle Low German stēgelitse, both eventually from Old Czech stehlec.

parole.significato: to disturb, to confuse or irritate, to interfere, to make noise
parole.testo: From German stören and/or Middle Low German stö̂ren, both from Proto-West Germanic *staurijan.

From older tylp, tylpel, from archaic German Tülpel (equivalent to present-day German Tölpel), from Middle Low German dorper. Doublet of torpare. Regarding the shift in sense from "villager" to "oaf", compare with the origin of the otherwise unrelated French vilain.
